newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Kabila said out of Zaire talks, returning to base.
newsitem.headline: Kabila said out of Zaire talks, returning to base.

text.p: Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila pulled out of an international peace summit intended to bring him into negotiations with President Mobutu Sese Seko on Friday, an official source in Angola said.
The source told Reuters that Kabila would not join Mobutu and South African President Nelson Mandela aboard a navy ship off the coast of Central Africa as earlier planned.
He said South African Deputy President Thabo Mbeki "has gone back to the boat to explain that Kabila is not coming tonight. Kabila is not happy with the arrangements. I can't go into what that is".

"My understanding is that Kabila is leaving or has left already for (Zairean rebel headquarters city of) Lubumbashi. We'll try to reconstruct this whole thing later, but obviously it's going to be very difficult," he said.
In Washington, a State Department spokesman said the United States was not confident the Kabila-Mobutu meeting would take on Friday and urged the two men to hold the talks.

"These talks are very important for President Mobutu, very important for alliance leader Kabila. But most importantly, very important for the people of Zaire. We believe it is essential that these talks take place. And we urge the leaders to make that happen," spokesman John Dinger told reporters.
Kabila's change of mind was the latest serious snag to hit the preparations for the talks proposed to end a seven-month-old rebellion against Mobutu's 32-year rule.

The rebel chief, whose forces have captured about three quarters of the vast country, has insisted that he is ready only to discuss Mobutu's immediate departure from power. The president's aides have said Mobutu wants to discuss a transition period leading up to elections.

Mbeki's jet left Luanda Airport at 18.05 p.m. (1705 GMT) for Pointe Noire in Congo where he was expected to join up with international envoys trying to broker peace talks between Zaire's warring sides on board a South African naval ship, the SAS Outeniqua.

Diplomatic sources told Reuters that Mandela was becoming frustrated by the delays leading up to the planned face-to-face peace talks between Mobutu and Kabila. The sources reported Mandela as saying: "We need to stop wasting time."
Despite international efforts to find a peaceful solution, the rebels were massing forces in areas closest to the capital Kinshasa, the only major city still under control of Mobutu's troops.
